pos: adj. (steadfast; unwavering; firmly fixed in purpose or practice)
etymology: Latin constans, from con- and stare, to stand together, stand firm — that which does not shift under pressure.
biblical_def:
Moreover I will establish his kingdom for ever, if he be constant to do my commandments and my judgments, as at this day.

David speaks these words to Solomon, handing on both the promise of an everlasting kingdom and the condition attached to its present enjoyment: constant obedience, not occasional compliance. The margin notes the Hebrew sense is literally strong, tying constancy to inward fortitude rather than mere habit — Solomon will need strength of resolve, not just good intentions, to keep commandments he has not yet been tested by. The verse holds together, without resolving the tension for the reader, an unconditional promise of an everlasting house and a conditional call to constant obedience, the same tension that runs through the entire Davidic covenant until it is finally and fully kept in Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONSTANS (L.): firm; steadfast; unchanging in purpose; not fickle or wavering.
webster_full: CONSTANT, a. Fixed; unchangeable; steadfast; firm in resolution or affection.
Implies inward strength of will, not merely outward repetition.
In 1 Chronicles, the condition David attaches to Solomon's enjoyment of the kingdom.
Carries the Hebrew sense of strong, not merely habitual.
Holds an unconditional promise and a conditional call in the same breath.
scriptures: Moreover I will establish his kingdom for ever, if he be constant to do my commandments and my judgments, as at this day.
corruption_summary: A soft therapeutic reading of covenant promises drops the if entirely, treating God's unconditional commitments as excusing any laxity in obedience, while David pairs the everlasting promise with a demand for constant, strong-willed faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to seize only the establish his kingdom for ever half of this verse and discard the if he be constant half as legalistic residue. David does not treat the two as in tension to be resolved by dropping one side.

The corrective is to read constant as David meant it — strength of resolve, not perfection achieved in one's own power — while recognizing that Solomon's own later failures, and the whole line of kings after him, prove that only one greater than Solomon could finally supply the constancy the covenant required.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazaq, to be strong, firm, resolute — the same root used of strengthening the hands for battle or work, here applied to moral and covenantal resolve.
roots_lines: Constant here carries the sense of strong, not merely habitual.
David attaches it as the condition for enjoying the promised kingdom.
The verse holds unconditional promise and conditional demand together.
Solomon's own later failures expose the limits of human constancy.
Only Christ finally supplies the constancy the covenant required.
usage: If he be constant to do my commandments and my judgments.
Carries the sense of strong resolve, not mere habit.
The Davidic covenant's tension of promise and condition in miniature.

pos: adj. (set apart as one; remarkable, extraordinary, distinguished from the ordinary)
etymology: Latin singularis, from singulus, one, single — that which stands apart from the common run of things.
biblical_def:
Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation.

Leviticus 27 regulates vows of a particularly weighty kind — a singular vow, one extraordinary enough to involve dedicating a person's value to the LORD rather than an animal or ordinary possession. The chapter immediately supplies a schedule of valuations by age and sex, converting an extraordinary, emotionally-charged vow into something administered with the same careful, impartial precision as any other transaction in Israel's worship. Singular marks the vow as exceptional in kind, but the law's response to the exceptional is not to treat it as beyond regulation; even the most extraordinary devotion to the LORD is to be honored through ordinary, orderly, accountable means.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SINGULARIS (L.): single; particular; remarkable; distinguished from others by some unusual circumstance.
webster_full: SINGULAR, a. Single; individual; remarkable; uncommon; distinguished from others.
Used of a vow of unusual or extraordinary weight.
Specifically, a vow dedicating a person's value to the LORD.
Leviticus 27 immediately regulates it with a precise valuation schedule.
Even extraordinary devotion is honored through ordinary, accountable means.
scriptures: Lev 27:2
Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation.
corruption_summary: Spiritual enthusiasm today often assumes an extraordinary vow or commitment should bypass ordinary accountability, while Leviticus 27 immediately subjects even a singular vow to a careful, impartial valuation schedule.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to treat the intensity of a singular vow as its own justification, exempt from the checks that govern ordinary commitments. The law disagrees: the very next verses supply exact valuations by age and sex, refusing to let extraordinary zeal escape ordinary, careful administration.

The corrective is to recover accountability as the companion of devotion, not its enemy: a vow's sincerity is not measured by how unregulated it is permitted to remain, but by whether the devoted person submits even extraordinary commitments to the LORD's own ordered means of honoring them.
roots_summary: Hebrew pala, to be extraordinary, difficult, wonderful — the same root behind pele, wonder, and Isaiah's Wonderful Counsellor, here marking a vow as exceptional rather than routine.
roots_lines: Singular marks a vow as exceptional, not ordinary.
Leviticus 27 specifically concerns vows dedicating a person's value.
An exact valuation schedule immediately follows by age and sex.
Extraordinary devotion is still subject to ordinary accountability.
Zeal and careful administration are not presented as opposites.
usage: When a man shall make a singular vow — an extraordinary, weighty commitment.
The persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation — regulated, not unregulated, devotion.
Even extraordinary vows are honored through ordered, accountable means.

pos: adj. (in general circulation and accepted value; passing readily as valid payment)
etymology: Latin currens, running, from currere, to run — money that runs freely in trade, accepted without question by all parties.
biblical_def:
And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.

This careful, almost legal detail closes the purchase of the cave of Machpelah, Abraham's only permanent possession of land in the whole of his sojourning in Canaan. Current money with the merchant specifies that the silver was weighed, not merely counted — standard, verified, universally acceptable payment, witnessed publicly in the audience of the sons of Heth, leaving no room for later dispute about the transaction's legitimacy. The word matters because the promise of the land was vast and future, but Abraham's actual possession of it, by faith, began with this single, scrupulously documented, fully-paid field — the first physical down payment on an inheritance his descendants would not fully receive for centuries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CURRENT: passing from hand to hand; generally received as valid; in common circulation as money.
webster_full: CURRENT, a. Passing from person to person; generally received and circulated.
Applied specifically to money accepted at standard, verified value.
Used in Genesis of Abraham's weighed, witnessed payment for Machpelah.
Distinguishes verified, public payment from an informal or disputed exchange.
Marks Abraham's first literal possession of the promised land.
scriptures: And Abraham hearkened unto Ephron; and Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver, which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.
corruption_summary: A spiritualized reading that rushes past this transaction as mere ancient-world detail misses its careful legal precision, which Scripture includes deliberately to anchor a vast future promise in a single, fully-documented, present possession.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be easy to treat the weighing of current money with the merchant as incidental narrative filler on the way to more exciting events. Genesis instead lingers over the detail, naming the price, the witnesses, and the standard of payment with evident care.

The corrective is to see the precision as theological, not merely historical: faith in God's vast future promise (the whole land, to innumerable descendants) is here expressed through scrupulous, present, verifiable action — a single field, honestly purchased, publicly witnessed, fully paid in current coin.
roots_summary: Hebrew over la-socher, literally passing to the merchant or trader, the technical phrase for silver accepted at full, standard trading value rather than merely weighed informally.
roots_lines: Current describes money accepted at standard, verified value.
Abraham weighs, rather than merely counts, the silver.
The transaction is witnessed publicly by the sons of Heth.
This is Abraham's first literal possession of the promised land.
A vast future promise is anchored in one scrupulously documented purchase.
usage: Four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.
Weighed, not merely counted, and witnessed publicly.
Faith expressed through present, verifiable, honest action.

pos: adj. (highest in authority or rank; superior to all other power)
etymology: Latin supremus, superlative of superus, upper — that which stands above every other rank or office.
biblical_def:
Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme.

Peter writes this to believers scattered under Roman rule, under an emperor who would soon unleash real persecution against the church, and the command is nonetheless unqualified: submit, for the Lord's sake, to the king as supreme. Supreme here is carefully bounded, not absolute — the civil ruler is supreme among human authorities, not supreme over God himself, and the same Peter had already told the Sanhedrin we ought to obey God rather than men when the two commands conflicted. The verse holds together ordinary submission to civil order as a positive Christian duty and the unstated but presupposed limit that no earthly supreme authority can claim what belongs to God alone.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SUPREMUS (L.): highest in power or authority; superior to all others; chief.
webster_full: SUPREME, a. Highest in authority; superior to all others; chief; paramount.
Here used of civil authority, specifically the Roman emperor.
Bounded implicitly by the higher authority of God himself.
Commanded for the Lord's sake, not merely out of fear or convenience.
Written to believers under a ruler soon to persecute the church.
scriptures: Submit yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake: whether it be to the king, as supreme;
corruption_summary: Political discourse often treats civil submission and ultimate loyalty to God as a zero-sum conflict, but 1 Peter 2:13 holds genuine submission to supreme civil authority together with the unstated limit Peter himself lived by: obey God rather than men when the two conflict.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to read supreme in an absolute sense that would make civil disobedience to any ruler always wrong, or conversely to treat Peter's own later defiance of the Sanhedrin as license to dismiss civil submission generally. Neither extreme matches the text.

The corrective is to hold both halves of Peter's own example together: ordinary, willing submission to civil authority for the Lord's sake as the normal Christian posture, with the understood limit, demonstrated by Peter's own life, that no earthly supreme authority can command what belongs to God alone.
roots_summary: Greek hyperechonti, holding above, excelling, used of the one holding the highest position — a relative, not absolute, superlative, naming the highest among human offices.
roots_lines: Supreme here names the highest human civil authority, not an absolute.
Peter commands submission to it for the Lord's sake.
The command is written under a ruler soon to persecute believers.
God's own higher authority is presupposed, not denied.
Peter's own life models both submission and its proper limit.
usage: Whether it be to the king, as supreme — the highest human civil office.
Submit yourselves... for the Lord's sake — submission as positive duty.
Bounded implicitly by obedience to God when the two conflict.

pos: adj. (admitting light through; clear enough to see through entirely)
etymology: Latin trans-, through, and parere, to appear — that through which light and sight pass unobstructed.
biblical_def:
And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.

John's vision of the New Jerusalem reaches for an impossibility to describe its reality: gold, the densest and most opaque of precious metals, rendered transparent like glass, clear enough to see through. The image refuses ordinary categories on purpose. Nothing in the fallen world offers gold this quality, and that is precisely why John must say as it were — straining human language to picture a purity so complete that even the street beneath the saints' feet has nothing hidden in it, nothing to obscure, substance and clarity united in a way earthly gold and earthly glass have never managed separately.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TRANSPARENT: having the property of transmitting light; clear; pervious to sight.
webster_full: TRANSPARENT, a. Having the quality of transmitting rays of light; pervious to sight.
Applied in Revelation to gold, an ordinarily opaque material.
Describes the street of the New Jerusalem.
An impossible combination in ordinary experience, used deliberately.
Pictures total purity: substance and clarity united without remainder.
scriptures: And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.
corruption_summary: A flattened literalism that tries to picture the New Jerusalem as ordinary gold rendered somehow see-through misses John's actual point: the image is deliberately impossible, straining language to describe a purity this world has no category for.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to treat transparent glass of gold as a riddle to be solved by some clever material science, as though John were describing an exotic but ultimately explicable substance. The text's own as it were signals the opposite: this is analogy reaching past its limits, not a specification.

The corrective is to let the impossibility stand as the message: the New Jerusalem's purity exceeds every earthly category of value and clarity simultaneously, gold without opacity, wealth without anything to hide, a city where nothing is both precious and obscured at the same time.
roots_summary: Greek hyalos, glass, paired with katharos, pure or clean — John combines a term for clarity with the standard word for gold to force an impossible, deliberately strained image.
roots_lines: Transparent describes an impossible combination: opaque gold made clear.
John's as it were signals strained, deliberate analogy.
The image describes the street of the New Jerusalem.
Purity this complete has no earthly category to contain it.
Wealth and clarity are united without remainder in the final city.
usage: The street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.
A deliberately impossible image, not a material riddle to solve.
Pictures a purity that exceeds every earthly category at once.

pos: adj. (deep; going to the depths; here, deeply committed to evil)
etymology: Latin profundus, from pro- and fundus, bottom — deep beyond the ordinary reach, applied here to depth of moral corruption rather than physical descent.
biblical_def:
And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all.

Hosea's charge against Israel's leadership uses profound in a startling, inverted way: not depth of wisdom or devotion, but depth of skill and commitment in rebellion and violence. The revolters have gone deep into their corruption, practiced and thorough in making slaughter, even while God himself has been a rebuker of them all, confronting their sin directly and repeatedly. The verse exposes a sobering possibility: a people can be profound, genuinely skilled and deeply invested, in exactly the wrong direction, and that depth of commitment to evil does not diminish but intensifies their guilt before a God who has not been silent about it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from PROFUNDUS (L.): deep; of great depth; figuratively, deeply skilled or thoroughly versed, here in evil.
webster_full: PROFOUND, a. Deep; of great depth, literally or figuratively.
Figuratively, thoroughly versed or skilled in some pursuit.
In Hosea, applied to depth of skill in making slaughter, not wisdom.
Paired with God's repeated, direct rebuke of the same people.
Exposes depth of commitment to evil as aggravating, not excusing, guilt.
scriptures: Hos 5:2
And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all.
corruption_summary: A culture that admires depth and commitment as virtues in themselves misses Hosea 5:2's warning that profound skill, applied to evil, is not impressive but doubly guilty, especially when God himself has already rebuked it.
corruption_paragraphs: It is tempting to treat profound as a neutral or even positive descriptor — depth of any kind sounding like a virtue. Hosea applies it to slaughter, forcing the reader to separate depth of commitment from the moral worth of what is being committed to.

The corrective is to weigh direction before depth: a profound skill in sin, pursued even in the face of repeated, direct divine rebuke, is not mitigated by its thoroughness but condemned more fully by it, because ignorance cannot be claimed where rebuke has already been given.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachat, to go deep, make deep, used here with a sense of thoroughness in wickedness, from a root also meaning to corrupt or destroy.
roots_lines: Profound here names depth of skill in evil, not wisdom.
Hosea applies it to the revolters' thoroughness in making slaughter.
God's repeated rebuke is set directly against this profound sin.
Depth of commitment to wrong intensifies, rather than excuses, guilt.
Direction, not merely depth, determines the moral worth of commitment.
usage: The revolters are profound to make slaughter — thoroughness in evil, not wisdom.
Though I have been a rebuker of them all — guilt compounded by prior warning.
Depth of skill in sin is condemned more fully, not excused, by its thoroughness.

pos: adj. (separated by a measured space; apart from another point by a fixed interval)
etymology: Latin distans, from dis- and stare, to stand apart — a fixed measure of space between two points.
biblical_def:
One board had two tenons, equally distant one from another: thus did he make for all the boards of the tabernacle.

This is as technical as Scripture gets: a carpentry specification for the tabernacle's framework, each board's two tenons set equally distant so that every board would fit uniformly into the silver sockets below. The word carries no theological freight by itself, and that is precisely the lesson worth drawing — the tabernacle where the glory of God would dwell among his people was built to exact, uniform tolerances, with no board permitted to be an exception to the measured standard. Distant here is load-bearing in the most literal sense: a structure meant to hold the weight of God's manifest presence could not be assembled from boards cut to each craftsman's preference.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISTANS (L.): separated in space; standing apart by a fixed or measured interval.
webster_full: DISTANT, a. Separated in space; remote; standing apart by an interval.
Used here as a precise carpentry specification, not a general description.
Describes the equal spacing of tenons on the tabernacle's boards.
Ensures uniform fit into the silver sockets beneath the framework.
A reminder that exact, uniform standards governed the dwelling place of God's glory.
scriptures: One board had two tenons, equally distant one from another: thus did he make for all the boards of the tabernacle.
corruption_summary: Nothing about this verse is doctrinally corrupted; the entry recovers a plain structural detail easy to skip in the long tabernacle-construction chapters, which readers often treat as the least rewarding part of Exodus.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is a technical carpentry term, not a theological one under cultural pressure.

The principle worth recovering is the seriousness with which Scripture treats exact conformity to a given pattern, even in a detail as unglamorous as tenon spacing — a seriousness that anticipates the New Testament's own insistence (Heb 8:5) that Moses was warned to make all things according to the pattern shewed thee in the mount.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashlaboth, set in order, paired with a measure of equal spacing — the term belongs to the tabernacle's technical construction vocabulary rather than its theological one.
roots_lines: Distant here is a precise carpentry specification, not a general term.
Each board's two tenons are set equally distant for uniform fit.
Every board of the tabernacle followed the same exact standard.
No craftsman's preference was permitted to vary the measure.
Exact conformity to the pattern governed even the smallest structural detail.
usage: One board had two tenons, equally distant one from another.
Thus did he make for all the boards of the tabernacle — uniform standard.
A structure for God's glory could not be built to varying tolerances.

pos: n. plural (fixed groupings of stars; here, celestial bodies whose light is withdrawn in judgment)
etymology: Latin constellatio, from con- and stella, star — a configuration of stars considered together as one body in the sky.
biblical_def:
For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine.

Isaiah's oracle against Babylon reaches for the most fixed, dependable features of the created order — stars, constellations, sun, moon — and pictures God simply switching them off. These are not minor lights but the very heavens the ancient world trusted as unchanging, used throughout Babylon's own astrological religion to read fate and fortune. The withdrawal of their light is total cosmic testimony: the God who made the constellations is not bound by them, cannot be read or controlled through them, and when he judges a proud empire, even the sky's most permanent fixtures answer to him rather than governing him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from CONSTELLATIO (L.): a cluster or group of fixed stars, considered as forming one figure or sign.
webster_full: CONSTELLATION, n. A group or cluster of fixed stars, forming a recognized figure.
Used by astrologers, especially in Babylon, to read omens and fortune.
In Isaiah, named among the created lights whose shining God withdraws.
Part of a sweeping oracle of judgment against Babylon's pride.
Testifies that even the fixed heavens answer to their Maker.
scriptures: For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine.
corruption_summary: Astrology's modern revival treats the constellations as governing or revealing human fate, precisely the claim Isaiah 13:10 overturns by picturing their Maker simply withdrawing their light when he judges the empire most devoted to reading them.
corruption_paragraphs: Babylon was the ancient world's capital of astrological religion, reading the constellations for guidance and omen. Isaiah's judgment oracle is aimed directly at that confidence: the very heavens Babylon trusted to govern events are shown to be simply switched off at their Maker's word.

The corrective for any renewed fascination with constellations as determiners of fate is this same demonstration: fixed stars are creatures, not governors, and their light shines or fails entirely at the decree of the God who assigned them their courses in the first place (Job 38:31-33).
roots_summary: Hebrew kesil, used elsewhere specifically of Orion (Job 9:9, 38:31, Amos 5:8), here in a plural construction for the constellations generally — the same root can also mean fool, an irony not lost on commentators regarding astrological confidence.
roots_lines: Constellations were central to Babylon's astrological religion.
Isaiah pictures God withdrawing their light entirely in judgment.
The oracle targets Babylon's pride and false confidence directly.
Fixed stars are shown to be creatures, not governors of fate.
Their shining depends entirely on their Maker's continuing decree.
usage: The stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light.
Part of a total cosmic judgment oracle against Babylon.
The fixed heavens answer to their Maker, not the reverse.

pos: n. (calmness; freedom from disturbance or trouble; settled peace)
etymology: Latin tranquillus, calm, quiet — a state free of the storms, literal or figurative, that disturb ordinary life.
biblical_def:
Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.

Daniel speaks these words to Nebuchadnezzar after interpreting the dream of the great tree, and the counsel is remarkable for both its boldness and its conditional hope: break off thy sins, show mercy to the poor, if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity. Daniel does not promise the judgment can be avoided — the text's own if signals genuine uncertainty — but he urges repentance anyway, for its own sake and for whatever mercy might follow, rather than assuming judgment once decreed is beyond any response. Tranquillity names the peace a proud king is about to lose, and Daniel's counsel shows a faithful servant warning power honestly while still hoping for its repentance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TRANQUILLUS (L.): calmness; quiet; a state of peace, undisturbed by trouble or agitation.
webster_full: TRANQUIL, a. Calm; quiet; peaceful; undisturbed.
TRANQUILLITY, n. The state of being tranquil; calmness; freedom from disturbance.
In Daniel, the peace Nebuchadnezzar is about to lose through judgment.
Daniel's counsel offers repentance as a conditional hope, not a guarantee.
Models a faithful servant warning power honestly while hoping for mercy.
scriptures: Dan 4:27
Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.
corruption_summary: A fatalistic reading of prophetic judgment can assume repentance is pointless once a warning has been given, but Daniel still counsels the king toward righteousness and mercy, offering tranquillity's lengthening as a genuine, if uncertain, hope.
corruption_paragraphs: It would be easy for Daniel, having just interpreted a dream of certain coming judgment, to conclude that counsel is wasted on a man already doomed to seven years as a beast. He counsels him anyway, break off thy sins by righteousness, refusing to treat prophecy as license for fatalism.

The corrective is Daniel's own modeled hope: if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity holds open a door even to a pagan king under pronounced judgment, a pattern consistent with God's dealings throughout Scripture (Jonah's Nineveh is the clearest parallel) where warned judgment and genuine opportunity for repentance are never presented as contradictions.
roots_summary: Aramaic shelevah, quietness, rest, prosperity — the state of untroubled wellbeing a king especially prizes, here offered as conditionally extendable through repentance.
roots_lines: Tranquillity names the untroubled peace Nebuchadnezzar currently enjoys.
Daniel counsels repentance even after pronouncing coming judgment.
The hope offered is genuine but explicitly conditional, not guaranteed.
Mercy to the poor and righteousness are named as the specific remedy.
Pronounced judgment and a real call to repentance are not contradictions.
usage: Break off thy sins by righteousness... if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.
Daniel's bold, hopeful counsel to a king under pronounced judgment.
Warned judgment and genuine opportunity for repentance held together.

pos: n. (a being carried or removed from one place or state to another, here from earth to heaven without death)
etymology: Latin translatio, from trans-, across, and ferre, to carry — a carrying across from one state of existence to another.
biblical_def:
By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.

Enoch's translation is the Old Testament's own anticipation of a hope the New Testament will later generalize to every believer: removal from this life into God's presence without passing through death at all. The writer to the Hebrews is careful about the order of events — for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God — making plain that the translation was the reward of a settled walk with God (Gen 5:24, walked with God, and he was not), not an isolated miracle detached from the character it crowned. Translation here stands as a down payment on the resurrection hope: proof within the Old Testament itself that God has power to remove his people from death's reach entirely, whenever and however he chooses.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from TRANSLATIO (L.): removal from one place or state to another; here, removal from earthly life to heaven without death.
webster_full: TRANSLATE, v.t. To remove from one place or condition to another.
TRANSLATION, n. The act of translating; a removal or transfer.
In Hebrews, specifically removal from earthly life without death.
Explicitly tied to Enoch's prior testimony of pleasing God.
Functions as an Old Testament anticipation of resurrection hope.
scriptures: Heb 11:5
By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.
corruption_summary: Fascination with Enoch's translation can drift toward speculative curiosity about where he went or what he saw, while Hebrews keeps the emphasis squarely on the faith and the settled, pleasing walk with God that preceded and explained it.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular curiosity about Enoch tends to chase extra-biblical speculation about his translation's destination or circumstances. Hebrews 11 is notably restrained, offering no such detail and instead doubling back to the testimony that preceded the event.

The corrective is to let the text's own emphasis stand: by faith Enoch was translated, and the faith is defined by a settled, long walk of pleasing God, not by the spectacular nature of his removal. The event crowns a character; it is not presented as interesting apart from it.
roots_summary: Hebrew laqach, to take, from Genesis 5:24 (God took him), rendered in the Septuagint and here in Hebrews with the Greek metetethe, to transfer or change place — the same root used of changing the priesthood in Hebrews 7:12.
roots_lines: Translation names removal from life to God's presence without death.
Hebrews ties it explicitly to Enoch's prior testimony of pleasing God.
The event crowns a settled character rather than standing apart from it.
It functions as Old Testament proof of God's power over death itself.
Later believers' resurrection hope has its root anticipation here.
usage: By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death.
Before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.
An Old Testament down payment on the full resurrection hope to come.
